name: Geiger counters and radiation survey meters
summary: Handheld meter that clicks or counts when ionising radiation passes through its tube, and shows counts per minute or a dose rate in µSv/h or mR/h.
uses: Higher-energy gamma and X-rays pass the case; alpha, beta and low-energy gamma get in only through the thin mica window, held close to the surface (IMI Inspector)
Alpha is stopped by a film of water, dirt, blood or clothing, and some Geiger counters can't see alpha or weak beta at all (ORISE REAC/TS)
Counts (CPM) are the direct reading. µSv/h is a gamma-only figure set for Cs-137, so it can be wrong for beta, alpha or other energies; one tube gives about 330 CPM per 1 µSv/h (IMI Inspector)
Normal background is about 0.05–0.2 µSv/h (CNSC INFO-0814); it rises with altitude and near granite, so take your own first (IMI Inspector). Canadians average about 1.8 mSv a year (CNSC background)
A tube doesn't respond equally at every gamma energy: one maker's curve reads several times high at tens of keV compared with above 300 keV (IMI Inspector)
In a very strong field a tube can overload and read zero or low even with a good battery (US patent 4,260,892); a quiet or low reading is never proof of safety
identify: A handheld box with a clicking speaker or flashing count light; the tube is inside or on a cable probe. A pancake probe is a flat round tube behind a mesh screen; the thin mica window under the screen lets alpha and weak beta in, and it is fragile (IMI Inspector). Digital units show CPM or CPS (counts) and µSv/h or mR/h (dose rate); 1 mR/h is about 10 µSv/h (IMI Inspector). Analogue meters have range settings and a battery check (ORISE REAC/TS). Old US civil-defence meters: the CD V-700 is a Geiger counter with a beta shield on its probe and a check source on the case (ORAU CD V-700 check sources); the CD V-715 is a high-range ion chamber for gamma only, with scales from 0–0.5 up to 0–500 R/h (ORAU CD V-715). Our arithmetic, not the museum's: even its lowest scale tops out near 5,000 µSv/h (taking 1 mR/h as about 10 µSv/h), so at normal background the needle should sit at or near zero. A calibration sticker shows the last check: in Canada a survey meter used for licensed work must have been calibrated within the past 12 months (NSRDR s.20). Alarm levels are set by the user; the IMI Inspector's default alert is 1 µSv/h (IMI Inspector).
test: 1. Battery: fit fresh cells, and on an analogue meter use the battery check to see the needle reach the battery band (ORISE REAC/TS). A battery left in for months can corrode it (IMI Inspector). 2. Window: visible breaks or wrinkles in the mica mean the tube needs replacing, and water can damage its coating (IMI Inspector). 3. Background: outdoors and away from granite, a Geiger counter gives a trickle of random clicks; ORISE expects about 20–100 counts a minute on its survey meters (ORISE REAC/TS). Average several one-minute counts and note the figure (ORISE REAC/TS). Over twice your own background is a CNSC portal-alarm level (CNSC INFO-0814): move away; don't hunt for the cause. No clicks for several minutes on the most sensitive range, speaker on, fresh battery: treat a Geiger counter as dead (our rule of thumb, not a maker's test). A normal trickle shows only that it is alive. A CD V-715 ion chamber is built for high levels, so a near-zero needle at background (our estimate) proves nothing. 4. Without a radioactive source: pour 5–10 g of potassium salt substitute onto paper; a thin-window (pancake) probe moved onto it should more than double the count; ORAU calls it a demonstration, not a calibrated check, and leftover salt raises background (ORAU salt substitutes). 5. Check source: on a CD V-700, open the beta shield, hold the probe on the spot on the case and read the x10 scale; 1.5–2.5 mR/h is a pass, but some of these sources have weakened (ORAU CD V-700 check sources). An electronic pulse test proves only the counting circuit, not the tube (IMI Inspector).

decay.note: Estimate. The maker says readings typically stay stable for many years; most failures come from batteries left in to leak, punctured or wet mica windows, and faded check sources (IMI Inspector; ORAU CD V-700 check sources). Ion chambers such as the CD V-715 drift when damp (ORAU CD V-715).

improvise: No meter: follow Canada's advice for a radiological emergency. Go inside at once, to the centre or basement away from doors and windows; close doors, windows and fireplace dampers; turn off fans and furnaces that draw in outside air; be ready to stay at least 24 hours; take potassium iodide only if public health tells you to (Get Prepared radiological). Use time, distance and shielding: less time near the source, as much distance as you can, and dense barriers such as concrete or lead (CNSC protecting workers). Alpha and beta can often be stopped by paper or plastic but do most harm inside the body, by being breathed in, swallowed or entering wounds, so keep dust off skin and out of food, lungs and cuts (CNSC INFO-0814). Some electronic personal dosimeters show dose rate and total dose, but not all models do, so don't treat one as a survey meter; a lab-read badge shows nothing (REMM detectors). The CNSC says unidentified radioactive material should be investigated only by people trained in radiation safety (CNSC INFO-0814): if you find something marked with the radiation symbol, leave it, keep people away, and never walk toward it to see whether your meter works.
